questions.stem: A home health nurse is visiting a 77-year-old client with heart failure. The client feels more tired than last week, the heart rate is 92/min, and the client says they are thirsty. Which finding is the most reliable sign of fluid retention?

options.text: A weight gain of 2 kg (4.4 lb) in the past 2 days
The client's report of more tiredness than last week
A resting heart rate of 92/min while sitting in a chair
The client's report of feeling thirsty most of the day

rationale.correct: Daily weight is the most reliable measure of fluid balance in heart failure.

perOption.a: Rapid weight gain is the most sensitive sign of fluid retention; 1 kg is about 1 L of fluid.
perOption.b: Fatigue is real but nonspecific.
perOption.c: A mildly fast heart rate has many causes.
perOption.d: Thirst does not reliably show fluid retention and may reflect diuretic use.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the best indicator of fluid retention in heart failure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure who takes lisinopril, spironolactone and furosemide is going home. Which self-care instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weigh yourself every morning after urinating, before breakfast, on the same scale
Report a gain of 1 to 1.5 kg (2 to 3 lb) in a day or 2 kg (5 lb) in a week
Report more shortness of breath or needing extra pillows to sleep
Use a salt substitute instead of table salt to flavor your meals at home
Skip the furosemide on days when your ankles and feet look normal
Drink at least 3 liters of water each day to protect your kidneys

rationale.correct: Heart failure self-care: daily weights, early warning signs, sodium limits, steady medication use, and no potassium salt substitutes with potassium-sparing drugs.

perOption.a: Consistent timing makes daily weights comparable.
perOption.b: These gains signal fluid retention that needs a treatment change.
perOption.c: Worsening dyspnea or orthopnea signals decompensation.
perOption.d: Most salt substitutes contain potassium, which can cause hyperkalemia with lisinopril and spironolactone.
perOption.e: Diuretics are taken as prescribed to prevent fluid buildup.
perOption.f: Many clients with heart failure need to limit fluids.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with a 40-pack-year smoking history comes to the emergency department short of breath and wheezing. The nurse hears diminished breath sounds but no crackles, and there is no ankle edema. The B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is 62 pg/mL. How should the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: Heart failure is unlikely to be the cause of the dyspnea
The result confirms early heart failure that needs diuretics
The result shows a pulmonary embolism is the most likely cause
The BNP is falsely low and should be repeated in the morning

rationale.correct: BNP helps tell cardiac from lung causes of dyspnea: below 100 pg/mL makes heart failure unlikely, and above about 400 strongly suggests it.

perOption.a: A BNP below 100 pg/mL makes heart failure an unlikely cause; a lung cause such as COPD is more likely.
perOption.b: A normal BNP points away from heart failure, so diuretics are not indicated by it.
perOption.c: BNP does not diagnose a pulmonary embolism.
perOption.d: There is no reason to doubt the result; it fits the clinical picture.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges

questions.stem: A client with acute pulmonary edema is extremely short of breath and anxious, with pink frothy sputum and an SpO2 of 84%. Oxygen is being applied. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: Lying flat on the back with the legs raised on pillows
Sitting upright with the legs hanging down
Lying on the left side with the head of the bed flat
Trendelenburg position to support blood pressure

rationale.correct: Sitting upright with the legs dependent reduces preload and improves lung expansion in pulmonary edema.

perOption.a: This increases venous return and worsens congestion.
perOption.b: Sitting upright with the legs dependent reduces venous return and eases breathing.
perOption.c: This does not reduce preload or help lung expansion.
perOption.d: A head-down position worsens pulmonary edema.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is being switched from lisinopril to sacubitril/valsartan. The last lisinopril dose was given at 0800 today. The client's potassium is 4.4 mEq/L and blood pressure 118/72. When can the first dose of sacubitril/valsartan be given?

options.text: With the evening medications at 2000 today
No sooner than 36 hours after the last lisinopril dose
After 7 days, once the lisinopril has fully cleared the body
As soon as tomorrow's potassium result is back

rationale.correct: An ACE inhibitor and an ARNI must never overlap; separate them by at least 36 hours.

perOption.a: Giving it the same day raises the risk of angioedema.
perOption.b: A 36-hour washout between an ACE inhibitor and sacubitril/valsartan lowers the risk of angioedema.
perOption.c: A week-long gap is not required and leaves the client untreated.
perOption.d: Potassium is monitored, but the washout period is the key rule.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply the washout rule when switching from an ACE inhibitor to sacubitril/valsartan.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure who takes spironolactone 25 mg and lisinopril 20 mg daily has a potassium of 5.9 mEq/L and peaked T waves on the monitor. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Potassium chloride ER 20 mEq orally daily
Furosemide 40 mg IV push now, then daily
A 2 g sodium diet with a 1.5 L fluid limit
Continuous cardiac monitoring on telemetry

rationale.correct: Spironolactone and ACE inhibitors both raise potassium; question any potassium supplement when hyperkalemia is present.

perOption.a: Giving potassium with hyperkalemia and ECG changes could cause a fatal dysrhythmia.
perOption.b: A loop diuretic helps remove potassium.
perOption.c: Sodium restriction is standard for heart failure.
perOption.d: Monitoring is appropriate with ECG changes.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Monitor potassium with potassium-sparing drug combinations.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the clinic note for a client with heart failure. Complete the sentence.

content.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {{b1}}, and the nurse should anticipate a prescription for {{b2}}.

options.text: an exacerbation of heart failure
community-acquired pneumonia
dehydration from poor intake
IV furosemide
a 1 L normal saline bolus
IV ceftriaxone

rationale.correct: Missed diuretic doses often trigger heart failure exacerbations; treatment focuses on diuresis and reducing preload.

perOption.b1:a: Weight gain, crackles, orthopnea and edema after missing the diuretic show fluid overload.
perOption.b1:b: There is no fever or productive cough to suggest infection.
perOption.b1:c: The findings show fluid excess, not a deficit.
perOption.b2:a: A loop diuretic removes excess fluid quickly.
perOption.b2:b: Extra fluid would worsen the overload.
perOption.b2:c: There is no sign of infection.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a heart failure exacerbation and its treatment.

exhibits.body: A 70-year-old with heart failure ran out of furosemide 5 days ago. Weight is up 2.7 kg (6 lb) since last week. Sleeps on 3 pillows. Crackles in both lung bases; 2+ ankle edema. Temperature 36.8 °C; SpO2 91% on room air.

questions.stem: A client is 4 hours after a total hip replacement. The surgical drain has filled twice in the last hour. Which finding is the earliest sign that the client is developing hypovolemic shock?

options.text: Blood pressure falling from 128/76 to 84/50 mm Hg in an hour
Heart rate up from 82 to 108/min with new restlessness
Urine output of 10 mL in the last hour
Mottled, cold skin over both knees and feet

rationale.correct: In early shock, compensation (tachycardia, vasoconstriction, anxiety) keeps the blood pressure normal; hypotension appears late.

perOption.a: Hypotension is a later sign that appears after compensation fails.
perOption.b: Tachycardia and restlessness appear early as the body compensates.
perOption.c: Very low urine output reflects established poor perfusion.
perOption.d: Mottling is a late sign.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize early compensated shock.

questions.stem: The ICU nurse is caring for five clients in shock. For each finding, choose the type of shock it is most consistent with.

rows.text: Flat neck veins and a falling hemoglobin after a gastrointestinal bleed
Crackles, distended neck veins and an S3 after a large anterior MI
Temperature 39.4 °C (103 °F), warm flushed skin and WBC 18,000/mm3
Blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg with a rising troponin after chest pain
Burns over 40% of the body with low urine output

rationale.correct: Hypovolemic = low volume (flat veins); cardiogenic = pump failure (congestion); septic = infection with vasodilation (warm skin early).

perOption.r1:c1: Blood loss reduces circulating volume, so the neck veins flatten.
perOption.r1:c2: Cardiogenic shock causes distended neck veins.
perOption.r1:c3: Sepsis does not directly lower hemoglobin.
perOption.r2:c1: Volume loss does not cause crackles or JVD.
perOption.r2:c2: A failing ventricle backs fluid into the lungs and veins.
perOption.r2:c3: Septic shock does not typically cause an S3 or JVD.
perOption.r3:c1: Hypovolemic shock causes cool, pale skin.
perOption.r3:c2: Cardiogenic shock causes cool, clammy skin.
perOption.r3:c3: Infection with vasodilation causes warm skin early in septic shock.
perOption.r4:c1: There is no fluid or blood loss.
perOption.r4:c2: Pump failure after MI causes cardiogenic shock.
perOption.r4:c3: There are no signs of infection.
perOption.r5:c1: Burn injury shifts large volumes of plasma out of the vessels.
perOption.r5:c2: Pump function is not the primary problem.
perOption.r5:c3: There is no infection at this stage.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with suspected urosepsis has a temperature of 39.1 °C, heart rate of 118/min and blood pressure of 94/58. The provider prescribes IV piperacillin-tazobactam, a lactate level and blood cultures. IV access is in place. What should the nurse do before starting the antibiotic?

options.text: Draw the blood cultures
Wait for the complete blood count results
Give acetaminophen to bring the fever down first
Insert an indwelling catheter for a urine culture

rationale.correct: Sepsis bundle: lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, and 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or a lactate of 4 mmol/L or more.

perOption.a: Cultures are drawn before antibiotics so the organism can be identified, without delaying the antibiotic.
perOption.b: Waiting delays lifesaving antibiotics.
perOption.c: Treating fever does not come before cultures and antibiotics.
perOption.d: A urine sample may be collected, but a catheter is not required before antibiotics.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Follow the sepsis bundle order.

questions.stem: A client with septic shock who weighs 154 lb has a blood pressure of 82/48 mm Hg, a heart rate of 124/min and a lactate of 4.6 mmol/L. The provider prescribes a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus. How many mL should the client receive in total?

rationale.correct: Weight: 154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg. Volume = 30 mL/kg × 70 kg = 2,100 mL.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Minutes after eating a cookie containing peanuts, a client has hives, wheezing, throat tightness and a blood pressure of 80/48 mm Hg. Which medication should the nurse give first?

options.text: Epinephrine 0.3 to 0.5 mg IM into the outer thigh
Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV push
Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV
Albuterol 2.5 mg by nebulizer for the wheezing

rationale.correct: Epinephrine IM is the first drug for anaphylaxis; it can be repeated every 5 to 15 minutes.

perOption.a: Epinephrine reverses bronchospasm and vasodilation and is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
perOption.b: Antihistamines are second-line and do not treat airway swelling or shock.
perOption.c: Steroids act slowly and are only adjuncts.
perOption.d: Albuterol helps wheezing but does not treat shock or airway edema.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Give the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: Four hours after coronary artery bypass surgery, a 66-year-old client's mediastinal chest tube drainage suddenly drops from 100 mL/hr to almost none. The blood pressure is 78/56 mm Hg, the neck veins are distended and the heart sounds are muffled. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Cardiac tamponade
Hypovolemic shock
Tension pneumothorax
Acute pulmonary embolism

rationale.correct: Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds) signals tamponade; prepare for pericardiocentesis or a return to surgery.

perOption.a: Hypotension, JVD and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) after a sudden drop in drainage suggest blood collecting around the heart.
perOption.b: Hypovolemia causes flat, not distended, neck veins.
perOption.c: This causes absent breath sounds on one side and tracheal shift, not muffled heart sounds.
perOption.d: PE does not cause muffled heart sounds.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cardiac tamponade.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old client who had a viral illness last week has sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breaths and lying flat. The ECG shows ST elevation in most leads. Which finding is most consistent with acute pericarditis?

options.text: Chest pain that eases when the client sits up and leans forward
Chest pain that goes away within minutes of nitroglycerin
Chest pain that spreads to the left arm only during exertion
Chest pain with a new murmur and splinter hemorrhages

rationale.correct: Pericarditis: sharp, pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, a pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation.

perOption.a: Leaning forward pulls the inflamed pericardium away from the heart and eases the pain.
perOption.b: This suggests angina.
perOption.c: This suggests ischemia.
perOption.d: These suggest endocarditis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the signs of pericarditis.

questions.stem: A client with a history of injection drug use is admitted with fever and fatigue. Infective endocarditis is suspected. Which findings support this diagnosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: A new heart murmur
Splinter hemorrhages under the nails
Painless red spots on the palms and soles
A barrel-shaped chest
A friction rub that eases when leaning forward
Bilateral ankle edema that worsens by evening

rationale.correct: Endocarditis shows fever, a new murmur and embolic signs (splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots).

perOption.a: Vegetations damage the valves and cause new murmurs.
perOption.b: These come from small emboli.
perOption.c: Janeway lesions are emboli to the skin.
perOption.d: A barrel chest is associated with COPD.
perOption.e: A friction rub points to pericarditis.
perOption.f: This is not a typical finding of endocarditis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize signs of infective endocarditis.

questions.stem: A client is going home after a mechanical mitral valve replacement and is starting warfarin. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take warfarin for as long as I have this valve."
"I'll tell my dentist about the valve before any dental work."
"I can stop the warfarin once my incision heals."
"I'll get my INR checked as often as I'm told."

rationale.correct: Mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin with INR monitoring, plus endocarditis prophylaxis before certain procedures.

perOption.a: Mechanical valves need lifelong anticoagulation.
perOption.b: Clients with prosthetic valves need antibiotic prophylaxis before some dental procedures.
perOption.c: Stopping warfarin risks clots on the valve and stroke.
perOption.d: Regular INR checks are needed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with severe aortic stenosis reports chest pain while walking to the bathroom. Blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula if SpO2 is below 90%
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual now
12-lead ECG during the chest pain
Troponin level now and in 3 hours

rationale.correct: In severe aortic stenosis, vasodilators such as nitroglycerin are used with great caution because they can cause a sharp fall in blood pressure.

perOption.a: Oxygen for hypoxemia is appropriate.
perOption.b: Clients with severe aortic stenosis depend on preload; nitrates can cause severe hypotension and syncope.
perOption.c: An ECG is appropriate for chest pain.
perOption.d: Serial troponins are appropriate to assess for ischemia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the risk of nitrates in aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: A client has a blood pressure of 224/132 mm Hg with a severe headache, blurred vision and new protein in the urine. A nicardipine infusion is started. What is the goal for the first hour of treatment?

options.text: Bring the blood pressure below 120/80 mm Hg as quickly as possible
Lower the mean arterial pressure by no more than about 25%
Keep the pressure where it is and treat the headache
Switch to oral medicine and recheck the pressure tomorrow

rationale.correct: In a hypertensive emergency, lower the MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then gradually toward 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours.

perOption.a: Lowering the pressure too fast can cause ischemia of the brain, heart and kidneys.
perOption.b: Gradual lowering protects organs used to high pressures.
perOption.c: End-organ damage needs treatment now.
perOption.d: A hypertensive emergency needs IV medication and close monitoring.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Set safe goals for treating a hypertensive emergency.

questions.stem: A client with a hypertensive emergency has been on an IV nitroprusside infusion at a high rate for 3 days because other drugs did not work. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?

options.text: A blood pressure of 148/88 mm Hg this morning
New confusion with metabolic acidosis
An opaque cover over the IV bag and tubing
A heart rate of 88/min and SpO2 of 96%

rationale.correct: Nitroprusside breaks down into cyanide; watch for confusion and acidosis, protect it from light, and monitor the pressure continuously.

perOption.a: This is an expected treatment response.
perOption.b: These suggest cyanide toxicity, a risk with prolonged or high-dose nitroprusside.
perOption.c: Nitroprusside is protected from light, so this is correct.
perOption.d: These values are acceptable.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize nitroprusside toxicity.

questions.stem: A client is 3 hours past coronary artery bypass graft surgery. Which finding should the nurse report to the surgeon?

options.text: Mediastinal chest tube drainage of 150 mL/hr for 2 hours
A temperature of 36.2 °C (97.2 °F) on arrival from surgery
Pain at the sternal incision rated 5 out of 10
Serosanguineous drainage in the chest tube

rationale.correct: Excessive chest tube drainage after cardiac surgery suggests bleeding and needs the surgeon's evaluation.

perOption.a: Drainage of more than 100 to 150 mL/hr for 2 hours or more suggests hemorrhage.
perOption.b: Mild hypothermia is common right after surgery and is treated with warming.
perOption.c: Moderate incision pain is expected.
perOption.d: Serosanguineous drainage is expected early.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with Raynaud phenomenon how to prevent attacks. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll wear gloves to take food out of the freezer."
"I'll cut down to two cigarettes a day."
"I'll limit coffee and other caffeine."
"I'll try relaxation to manage my stress."

rationale.correct: Raynaud teaching: avoid cold, nicotine, caffeine and stress, which all cause vasospasm.

perOption.a: Cold triggers vasospasm, so gloves are appropriate.
perOption.b: Any nicotine causes vasoconstriction; stopping completely is needed.
perOption.c: Caffeine can cause vasoconstriction.
perOption.d: Stress can trigger attacks.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client with peripheral arterial disease gets calf pain after walking one block. The provider recommends a walking program. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Walk until the pain starts, rest until it eases, then walk again."
"Avoid walking any distance that brings on the calf pain, to protect the leg."
"Raise your legs above heart level whenever you rest."
"Wear tight compression stockings when you go for walks."

rationale.correct: For PAD: walk to claudication, rest, and repeat, for 30 to 45 minutes about 3 times a week.

perOption.a: Walking to the point of claudication builds collateral circulation.
perOption.b: Exercise to the point of pain improves walking distance.
perOption.c: Elevation reduces arterial flow; legs should be level or slightly down.
perOption.d: Compression can further reduce arterial flow.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach an exercise program for peripheral arterial disease.

questions.stem: A client recovering from an uncomplicated myocardial infarction 10 days ago asks when it is safe to resume sexual activity. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Most people need to wait at least 6 months after a heart attack."
"Usually once you can climb two flights of stairs without symptoms."
"It's safest for your heart to avoid sexual activity from now on, to be sure."
"Taking sildenafil beforehand will help protect your heart."

rationale.correct: Many clients can resume sexual activity when they tolerate moderate exertion, such as two flights of stairs, often 1 to 2 weeks after an uncomplicated MI.

perOption.a: Most clients can resume much sooner.
perOption.b: Tolerating this level of exertion suggests sexual activity is likely safe; the provider confirms.
perOption.c: This is inaccurate and harms quality of life.
perOption.d: Sildenafil does not protect the heart and is dangerous with nitrates.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The home health nurse documents a visit with a 74-year-old client who has heart failure. Highlight the findings that indicate worsening heart failure.

segments.text: "I had to sleep in my recliner the last two nights."
Weight is up 1.8 kg (4 lb) since 2 days ago.
New crackles in both lung bases.
Ate a frozen dinner and canned soup yesterday.

rationale.correct: Orthopnea, rapid weight gain and new crackles signal decompensation.

perOption.s2: Needing to sleep upright (orthopnea) signals worsening pulmonary congestion.
perOption.s4: Rapid weight gain shows fluid retention.
perOption.s8: Crackles show fluid in the lungs.
perOption.s10: This is a controlled blood pressure.
perOption.s12: High-sodium food is a risk to address, but it is not itself a sign of worsening.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize worsening heart failure during a home visit.
